content: The kilometer, also spelled kilometre in British English, is a unit of length in the metric system. It is equivalent to one thousand meters, with the meter being the current SI base unit of length. In scientific notation, a kilometer can be expressed as 1 × 10³ meters (engineering notation) or 1E+3 meters (exponential notation), both of which signify 1,000 meters. The corresponding unit of area derived from the kilometer is the square kilometer, while the corresponding unit of volume is the cubic kilometer. The pronunciation of kilometer varies, with one common pronunciation following the stress pattern used for measuring instruments like barometer, thermometer, tachometer, and speedometer. This stress pattern is not typically applied to other metric measurements such as millimeter or centimeter. Colloquial terms for the kilometer include click (sometimes spelled klick or klik) and kay (or simply k). These informal terms can also refer to kilometers per hour, which is abbreviated as km/h, km h⁻¹, km·h⁻¹, or informally as kph. Additionally, the term kilometrage may be used in a similar context to mileage. Internationally, the United Kingdom and the United States are the only two developed nations that have not transitioned their road signs from miles to kilometers. In the UK, this is due to the continued use of imperial units such as miles, yards, and inches, as well as the cost of replacing speed signs, which cannot be changed during routine maintenance for safety reasons. As of September 11, 2007, the European Union has allowed Britain to continue using the imperial system. EU Commissioner Günter Verheugen stated, There is not now and never will be any requirement to drop imperial measurements. In the United States, the National Highway System Designation Act of 1995 prohibits the use of federal highway funds to convert existing signs or purchase new signs with metric units. However, since 2000, the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices has been published in both metric and American customary units.
